Where it began

Josh Hazlewood was born in Tamworth on 8 January 1991 and grew up in Bendemeer, a small country town about 40 km to the north. He was the youngest of three, and his cricket was forged in fierce backyard contests with his older brother.

Those battles clearly worked. By 12 he was turning out for Tamworth against grown men, and at 17 he was picked for New South Wales, the youngest fast bowler the state had ever chosen. He made his first-class debut at the Sydney Cricket Ground against New Zealand in November 2008.

The player

His Test debut came against India at the Gabba in December 2014, and he marked it with five wickets in the first innings. A year later he was named player of the match in the first day-night Test ever played, against New Zealand, taking the first wicket and the first five-wicket haul under lights. That match also took him to 50 Test wickets in only his 12th Test.

He took 20 wickets in the 2019 Ashes in England, and in August 2026, against Bangladesh, he became the 9th Australian to reach 300 Test wickets. By November 2026 he had played 80 Tests and taken 311 wickets at 23.85, with 15 five-wicket hauls and a best of 6 for 49.

What made him special

Accuracy was everything. He hit a length and stayed there, and the comparisons with Glenn McGrath followed naturally. In 2021 he became the first bowler to sit in the top ten of the ICC rankings in all three formats at once.

With the bat he was a willing tail-ender rather than a dangerous one, with 582 Test runs and a best of 39. His 51 not outs in 102 innings, though, show he was very hard to get out, which is half the job.

Away from the middle

He won the 2015 and 2023 World Cups and the 2021 T20 World Cup with Australia, was the ICC's Emerging Cricketer of the Year in 2015, and led Australia in a one-day international in 2022. In the IPL he helped Royal Challengers Bengaluru to their first title in 2025, holding his nerve in the final over of the final to defend the total and win by six runs. As a boy he followed the Newcastle Knights in rugby league.

And finally

In a one-day match against New Zealand in 2017 he shared a stand of 54 for the last wicket with Marcus Stoinis, lasting 26 minutes, without facing a single ball. He was then run out at the non-striker's end. Up to that point he had gone 33 one-day internationals without ever being dismissed, a record, which tells you how seldom anyone managed it.
